Police officer seen helping drug dealer Raja escape in CCTV footage
item.description:
CCTV footage has emerged showing how Raja, alias “Picchi Raja”, a suspected drug dealer from Mohammadpur, escaped from a prison van in Dhaka, with police investigators saying an officer helped him get out of the vehicle.
Several CCTV clips obtained on Tuesday evening show the prison van stopping on a busy road in Tantibazar at around 5:58pm on September 27.
The footage shows the rear door of the van being opened as it moved slowly through traffic. Three masked people then stepped out one after another — two accused persons and a police officer.
The prison van had left a Dhaka court that evening carrying 30 accused persons to Kashimpur Jail in Gazipur.
According to the police investigation, when the van reached the area in front of Popular Diagnostic Centre in Tantibazar, it slowed down amid a traffic jam. Sub-Inspector Probir Kumar Biswas, who was in charge of the van, opened the rear door, went inside, and brought out two accused persons.
The first was Raja. The second was Khairul Bashar, owner of Cambrian School and College.
CCTV footage shows Khairul, wearing a white shirt, getting off the van and walking onto the road alongside Raja. After walking a short distance, Khairul returned to the van within seconds and took a seat beside the driver.
Raja, however, continued walking. SI Probir Kumar Biswas, wearing a red shirt, can be seen following him.
Police said Raja was allowed to leave the van so he could meet family members and subsequently escape. Khairul was allegedly allowed to sit beside the driver because the van was air-conditioned.
Investigators said the plan to help Raja escape had been made two days before the incident. The van driver and Raja’s sister, Taslima, were allegedly involved in the plan.
SI Probir Kumar Biswas, van driver Naik Kamal Hossain and Taslima have been arrested in connection with the incident.
On Tuesday, Gazipur Metropolitan Magistrate Court Judge Zubayer Rashid granted four days of remand for the three accused.
Gazipur Metropolitan Police Commissioner Israil Howlader said at a press conference on Tuesday that several other people had also been found to be involved in Raja’s escape, including a private car driver and one of his close relatives.
However, police have not yet disclosed which vehicle Raja got into after leaving the prison van or where he went.
Law enforcement agencies have increased surveillance at different points along the country’s borders in an effort to arrest him, police said.
Raja was arrested at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka on May 19 while returning from Nepal with his wife and brother-in-law. He had been in jail in connection with several cases.

Experts: Survivor experiences, research can drive policy change on violence against women
item.description:
Turning research findings and survivor experiences into concrete policy and action could strengthen efforts to prevent and address violence against women and girls, speakers said at the ninth Sexual Violence Research Initiative (SVRI) Forum in Bangkok on Tuesday.
The opening plenary, titled “Evidence and Activism,” brought together researchers, advocates and survivor-leaders to discuss how evidence can be translated into advocacy and policy action during the four-day forum.
The forum is being held at the Centara Grand and Bangkok Convention Centre, bringing together more than 1,500 researchers, practitioners, survivors, funders and advocates from around the world.
SVRI Forum Co-Founder and Chair Dr Claudia Garcia Moreno said the growth of the forum reflected the wider growth of research and activism in the field.
“We want to continue the Forum being driven by science,” she said.
Olympic swimmer and survivor advocate Joanna Maranhão highlighted research showing that 63% of Brazilian athletes had experienced sexual violence before the age of 18.
“If justice is not for me I will make sure it is for other people,” she said, describing her experience of turning personal trauma and research findings into advocacy.
Another example came from Latin America, where survivor advocate Olimpia Coral Melo campaigned for legal recognition of digital violence after experiencing abuse herself.
Melo, founder of Defensoras Digitales de Latinoamérica, said support from people who believed in her helped her push for legislation that became known as Ley Olimpia, or Olimpia’s Law.
“Mine was a violence that wasn't visible, couldn't be touched, and didn't have a name,” she said, adding that it is now recognized as a crime under the survivor-led law.
Diane Kambanei, director of Papua New Guinea’s National Gender-Based Violence Secretariat, spoke about how research findings were used to strengthen advocacy for government action.
She said policy recommendations based on research helped advocates secure, for the first time, a dedicated share of the national budget for addressing gender-based violence.
“Before, GBV was a women’s issue, and now it’s a government issue,” Kambanei said.
The second day of the forum also featured sessions examining the links between climate change and violence against women and girls, including climate-related mobility and women’s leadership.
Another session explored the potential of rugby in Pacific communities as a platform for preventing violence against women and girls.
The program also included poster sessions and an SVRI Salon screening of “Being Family,” a drama made with migrant and displaced families living along the Thailand-Myanmar border.
The forum is focusing on research, survivor leadership and practical approaches to preventing violence, with discussions continuing through the program.

item.title: Guardians of the cage
item.description:
It was a cold, crisp, snowy day in February 1966 when in a New York City studio, a masterpiece of a song, "It's a Man's Man's Man's World" was co-written by James Brown and Betty Jean Newsome.
James Brown, who was then at the absolute peak of his commercial popularity, performed this song in live shows for the rest of his musical career.
The song starts with "This is a man's world" and goes on to aggressively ascribe all the works of the modern civilization such as cars, trains, boats, and electric light solely to male efforts; however, as if to pour oil on troubled waters, the song ends with a casual claim that it all would mean "Nothin' without a woman or a girl."
Interestingly, while Brown globally popularized the phrase "This is a man's world" through his "biblically chauvinistic" track, Newsome later claimed to have written the lyrics based on her own observations of gender dynamics.
Do you see the irony? This historic anthem that was profoundly criticized for its extreme machismo was given its meaning by Newsome, a woman herself, who fought for decades so her name was not erased from its history.
Sixty years ago, a phrase became universal due to the lyrical genius of a woman; the same phrase is still being used by our male-dominated society whenever patriarchy demands our women to be put in their “rightful” position.
In 1990, Sylvia Walby defined patriarchy as “a system of social structures and practices in which men dominate, oppress, and exploit women.” In other words, patriarchy is a system that predominantly favours men.
Yet, are men the only ones to forge ahead with patriarchy? Has it ever crossed your mind how women themselves, wearing the invisible cloak of patriarchy, have been perpetuating the faults of the system in the name of tradition all this time?
One bewildering characteristic of patriarchy is that it pits women against women. Each time a mother, a female teacher, a mother-in-law, a female friend, points the policing fingers at the woman next to her for not yielding to the system, the chain of patriarchy moves forward.
It is a common experience of girls growing up in Bangladesh to face judgement from women. The mechanism of patriarchy is so deeply rooted into our society that many women preach oppression instead of being a part of the sisterhood.
Remember the legendary cartoon Meena ? In this timeless children’s show, Meena’s mother and grandmother, clearly biased towards her brother Raju, would often discriminate between the siblings. Sadly, most girls born and growing up with brothers in Bangladeshi households are no stranger to this discrimination.
Unfortunately, the very first whip of patriarchy almost always comes from the mothers, who are often found policing their daughters’ bodies and behaviours so that the daughters conform to the entrenched norms of this patriarchal society.
Mothers often teach their daughters to adjust, to endure, to follow the rules, while their sons grow up knowing the world will negotiate the rules for them.
One survey showed that 93% families in Bangladesh see their sons as a blessing, while 96% see their daughters as a “problem” to the family and the country. The discrimination is reflected in dietary portions, permission to play outside, and the freedom to make friends.
This motherly discrimination is topped with the unwanted surveillance of the “aunty society.” The women from the neighbourhood or the mothers waiting outside schools and coaching centres almost invariably engage in tracking down girls for having male friends, talking or laughing too loud, dressing up, or wearing light makeup. These small acts of freedom often end up becoming the gravest of sins.
For many girls, even classrooms become a place for moral policing. Female teachers, who should be providing a safe outlet for the students, justify their humiliating remarks as “protection.” Moreover, in many co-ed institutions, female teachers sometimes show unfair preferences towards male students.
Among peers, women frequently face criticism disguised as opinions from other women, based on their life choices, work positions, or clothing.
Women who conform to societal expectations often feel superior and disdain women who choose to live lives that don’t align with those beliefs. Conformity thus turns into a currency for winning in life for women embodying patriarchy.
This submission to patriarchy continues as a mother-in-law’s abuse of her daughter-in-law activates the cycle of unjust treatment and passes it down from one generation to the next. As the mother of the groom, her actions of looking down on the bride's family and demanding dowry eventually turn into violence against the daughter-in-law.
And when the violent treatment compels the daughter-in-law to return to her parents’ house, it is often her mother who sends her back to her in-law’s house in the name of family honor. To these mothers, a dead daughter is far better than a divorced daughter.
So, should we consider these women culpable for the continuity of patriarchy? Before answering this question, we should ask a more important one: Why do women partake in this vile practice?
Denied direct power, as argued by author and academic Deniz Kandiyoti, many women learn to negotiate security by adapting to the system’s rules rather than resisting. Women submit to patriarchy as a survival mechanism and to gain authority over other women.
However, the consequences of this chain of patriarchy teach women to be each other’s judges instead of allies. It pierces through the sisterhood and hides structural patriarchy behind a facade of women blaming each other. Meanwhile, the system itself is perpetuated through whoever is closest to it.
To break through the shackles of patriarchy, women need to recognize the contradictions that make them the silent flag-bearers. Decoding the patterns can easily turn the contention into cohesion. This is why, when sisterhood refuses to become patriarchy’s ally, it motivates women to heal and grow together.
Nadia Afroze Disha is a lecturer at Brac Business School, Brac University. Purnasha Aurora is a student of Economics at Brac University.

Thailand floods death toll rises to 60 since mid-September
item.description:
Flooding in Thailand since mid-September has killed 60 people nationwide, the government said on Wednesday, with river water levels still rising in some regions.
Days of heavy rain late last month inundated parts of the capital Bangkok, although the floods there have largely receded.
The situation remains difficult for many people in central Prachinburi province, where 19 people died, according to the Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation.
Overflowing rivers flooded houses in seven districts in the province, affecting more than 188,000 people, the department said in a statement.
People have died in around a dozen other provinces and the capital, with flooding ongoing in 27 of Thailand’s 77 provinces, it said.
In Bangkok, four people have died since September 16, after a month’s worth of rain fell over several days in late September, prompting a city-wide disaster declaration.
A massive clean-up is currently underway as the city prepares to host the IMF and World Bank meetings, which begin next week.
Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul, whose government has faced public criticism over its flood response, ordered government agencies on Monday to manage flooding and transportation to avoid disruptions to the meetings.
September is the peak of Thailand’s rainy season, but this year felt worse for many in Bangkok, a city built on former marshlands and intersected by a network of canals.
Some areas were under knee-deep water for several days, with vehicles abandoned on submerged streets and schools closed for two days.

item.title: Yemen’s Houthis claim new attacks on Saudi airports as conflict deepens
item.description:
The Houthis claimed a flurry of attacks on Saudi targets on Wednesday including firing a ballistic missile at Riyadh airport, as the group battles for territory in Yemen against government forces supported by the kingdom.
The Houthis, who control most of northwest Yemen, captured swathes of coastal land from Yemen’s pro-government forces last month after the country’s civil war reignited in July.
The internationally recognized government this week declared a counter-offensive and claims to have uprooted Houthi fighters from strategic areas on the Red Sea and the port city of Mocha.
But the Iran-backed Houthis say they are holding their territory, and military sources from both sides contacted by AFP have not reported any major changes on the ground.
Claims by both sides have been impossible to independently verify with the situation moving fast and access for journalists difficult.
“Our armed forces have just targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with a ballistic missile. The strike was accurate, by God’s grace, and led to a disruption of air traffic,” Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said Wednesday in a post on X.
The Saudi-led military coalition that backs Yemen’s government said the missile was intercepted.
In a separate post the Houthis also said they targeted military supplies at a camp area near the airport in the Yemeni city of Aden, the interim capital for the government.
The Yemeni government’s Saba news agency reported missiles and drones targeting that airport.
Saree earlier said drones and missiles also targeted Saudi Arabia’s Abha airport and King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait and had “hit their targets accurately.”
It is the second time this week that the Houthis claimed to have attacked the main airport in the Saudi capital.
It is facing frequent temporary closures of its airspace, according to tracking website Flightradar24, but Saudi authorities have not publicly acknowledged the closures or confirmed any strikes targeting the facility.
Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that has been fighting the Houthis since 2015, and is now trying to roll back the group’s latest advance.
On Monday, the coalition said it was providing air support for the counter-offensive launched by the Yemeni government forces.
After a four-year ceasefire, Yemen’s civil war re-erupted in July. Last month the Houthis seized the entire western coastline along the Red Sea in the country’s deadliest fighting in years.
The renewed violence has also deepened the wider Middle East war, which has roiled world energy markets and snarled shipping routes in the region.
Yemen’s government has announced a goal of retaking all Houthi territory -- home to most of the country’s population, and much of it held for more than a decade.
On Tuesday sources on both sides told AFP that fighting across the country had killed more than 270 government troops and Houthi fighters over the past day alone.
The Yemen conflict has also caused a dire humanitarian crisis that left most of the nation’s population dependent on aid.
More than 184,000 people have been displaced by the latest fighting, according to the United Nations.
Mohammed, a 33-year-old charity worker who fled from Mocha to Aden, told AFP on Tuesday that “people there are terrified.”
“Life in Mocha has come to a complete standstill -- there is no movement at all. The city has become a war zone,” he said.

Nobel Peace Prize haunted by the ‘specter’ of Trump
item.description:
Donald Trump’s chances of winning the Nobel Peace Prize are seen as minimal, but his “specter” will cast its shadow over Friday’s announcement of the winner in Oslo, experts say.
The Norwegian Nobel Committee knows it will be under close scrutiny: Since his return to the White House in January 2025, the billionaire Republican has campaigned intensively for the prize and hasn’t hidden his disappointment at not winning it yet.
The chances of him getting the nod are however undermined by his war against Iran, his territorial ambitions -- sometimes at the expense of allies, as in Greenland -- and his attacks on international cooperation institutions and the media.
Even though he has not been lobbying as openly for the Nobel in recent weeks, Trump remains on everyone’s minds, with strong chances that the committee’s pick will, regardless of who they choose, be interpreted as direct or indirect criticism of the US president.
Trump is “the specter in the room,” said the head of the Peace Research Institute in Oslo (Prio), Haakon Gjerlow.
He said the Nobel committee must be asking itself: “Is there any potential for this prize to create harm rather than good in awarding it?” given the reactions that could emerge from the White House.
The Nobel Institute says it is unfazed.
“There’s always a lot of lobbying, and ultimately perhaps also attempts to exert pressure on the committee. So in one sense we’re very used to that,” the secretary of the committee, Kristian Berg Harpviken, told AFP.
“It’s not something we don’t discuss. Of course we have to discuss it, but it’s not like that influences the discussions in the room and decisions that come out,” he insisted.
Last year, the prestigious prize went to Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, a choice generally considered palatable to Trump.
Machado even gave him her Nobel gold medal, judging he deserved it after the capture of President Nicolas Maduro -- though she failed to obtain his political backing in exchange.
Those events could prompt the committee to this year choose a laureate who enjoys broad consensus, such as an individual or organization working to protect children or humanitarian efforts.
That could include the Save the Children charity and Mykola Kuleba, a Ukrainian children’s rights activist campaigning for the return of kids illegally taken to Russia from occupied territories -- a cause close to the heart of Trump’s wife Melania.
Sudan’s Emergency Response Rooms (ERR), a vast network of volunteers risking their lives to help people facing the double threat of war and hunger, could also be a potential laureate.
But the committee may also choose a laureate that could rub Trump the wrong way.
That could include the UN special rapporteur for the occupied Palestinian territories Francesca Albanese, Pope Leo XIV, press freedoms with an award to the Committee to Protect Journalists, or international justice bodies such as the International Criminal Court (ICC) and the International Court of Justice (ICJ).
“We live in an age of predators. We have Trump, Putin, Netanyahu,” said Nobel historian Asle Sveen.
“They don’t want to have an international order. They want to have big powers with spheres of influence. And this court stands in the way,” he said, referring to the ICC.
A total of 287 individuals and organizations have been nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize, though the names on the list are kept secret for 50 years.
But peace remains elusive in many parts of the world: 65 armed conflicts involving at least one state actor were registered in 2025, the highest number since 1946, according to PRIO.
“At an overall level, it is clear that the world is not developing in the right direction,” said Harpviken.
“At the same time ... there is no lack of good initiatives. There is no lack of organizations or individuals who do good work,” he said.
“A peace prize may make more sense than ever.”

item.title: UNHRC adopts first-ever resolution on AI; Bangladesh acts as penholder
item.description:
The United Nations Human Rights Council has adopted by consensus the first-ever resolution on artificial intelligence (AI), titled “Implications of Artificial Intelligence for the Promotion and Protection of Human Rights”, with Bangladesh serving as the penholder and playing a leading role in advancing the initiative.
During the ongoing 63rd session of the UN Human Rights Council, Bangladesh joined fellow Core Group members Algeria, Austria, Egypt, Greece, Guyana, Kuwait and Nepal in steering the initiative on AI and human rights.
Guided by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Bangladesh, the initiative was first presented before the Council in August 2026 by former Ambassador and Permanent Representative Nahida Sobhan on behalf of the Core Group.
Since then, the Core Group has pursued an open, inclusive and constructive process of engagement with Member States and relevant stakeholders.
The consensus adoption marks a significant step forward in strengthening the Council’s consideration of the evolving relationship between artificial intelligence and human rights, while keeping human dignity, development, inclusion and international cooperation at the centre.
It also reflects Bangladesh’s growing and constructive role in shaping international discussions at the intersection of emerging technologies, development and human rights, and its growing contribution to multilateral diplomacy.
Bangladesh underscored that continued constructive engagement and cooperation among Member States and stakeholders will remain essential as the initiative moves forward.

item.title: Dhaka air pollution worsens, ranks 3rd globally
item.description:
Dhaka ranked third among the world's most polluted cities on Wednesday morning, recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 173 at 10:10am.
The air quality was classified as ‘unhealthy’, meaning the concentration of pollutants in the air had reached a level that could pose health risks to the general population, according to the AQI scale.
Kuala Lumpur in Malaysia ranked first with an AQI score of 210, while Singapore in Singapore ranked second with a score of 176.
According to AQI standards, a reading between 101 and 150 is considered 'unhealthy for sensitive groups', while 151 to 200 is classified as 'unhealthy'. A reading between 201 and 300 is considered 'very unhealthy', while levels above 301 are deemed 'hazardous', posing serious health risks.
The AQI provides daily updates on air quality, indicating how clean or polluted the air is and highlighting potential health impacts.
In Bangladesh, the AQI is calculated based on five major pollutants: particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO2) and ozone.
Dhaka has long struggled with air pollution, with air quality typically deteriorating during winter and improving during the monsoon season.
The World Health Organization estimates that air pollution causes around seven million deaths globally each year, mainly from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer and acute respiratory infections.

item.title: LPG cylinders sell at Tk200-500 above govt-fixed price in Faridpur
item.description:
Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) cylinders are being sold at Tk200-500 above government-set prices in Faridpur, with consumers blaming inadequate market monitoring and alleged supply shortages.
The Bangladesh Energy Regulatory Commission (BERC) has raised the price of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), setting the price of a 12kg cylinder at Tk 1,837, up from Tk 1,585.
Consumers in Faridpur town, upazila headquarters, and remote markets said they are often forced to pay more than the fixed price despite LPG cylinders being available.
Depending on brand and size, cylinders are currently selling for Tk2,000-2,500 in different markets across the district, locals said. Prices are reportedly even higher in some remote markets in Nagarkanda, Saltha and Madhukhali.
Consumers said the rising cost of LPG is adding to the financial pressure on households already struggling with higher prices of essential commodities.
Two autorickshaw drivers, a hotel owner and a homemaker on Mujib Road in Faridpur town said authorities should strengthen market monitoring and ensure LPG is sold at the fixed price.
The price hike is also affecting small businesses, particularly hotels, restaurants, food shops and tea stalls that rely on LPG for cooking.
Several traders in Nagarkanda market said LPG costs more in village markets than at the upazila headquarters, increasing their operating expenses and reducing profits.
“Cooking costs are rising with the price of gas. Other essentials have also become more expensive. Overall, it has become difficult to run the business as before,” a hotel owner said.
Retailers, however, attributed the higher prices to supply shortages. They said they sometimes have to buy cylinders at higher prices and incur additional transportation costs, making it difficult to sell them at government-set rates.
“We are also buying gas at higher prices. When supply is irregular, we sometimes have to incur additional costs to collect cylinders. We do not want to charge customers more deliberately,” a retailer said.
Locals also alleged that regular monitoring by the Directorate of National Consumer Rights Protection was lacking despite widespread complaints of overpricing. They called for regular drives to ensure LPG is sold at government-set prices.
Faridpur Additional District Magistrate Susmita Saha said instructions had been issued to all upazila nirbahi officers and executive magistrates to monitor LPG prices.

Vegetable prices fall in Dinajpur, farmers struggle to recover production costs
item.description:
Vegetable prices have fallen in Dinajpur markets as supplies of early winter produce increase, bringing relief to consumers but leaving farmers worried about recovering production costs.
Prices of some vegetables have dropped by up to Tk30 per kg compared with last week. The trend was observed at Bahadur Bazar and other kitchen markets in Dinajpur town.
Supplies of winter vegetables, including red amaranth, spinach, radish greens, cabbage, cauliflower, beans, radish, carrots, tomatoes, turnips, beetroot, and capsicum, have increased significantly.
Imported green chillies are selling for Tk90-100 per kg, while locally produced chillies cost Tk130-140, down Tk20-30 from last week.
Potatoes are selling for Tk16-30 per kg depending on variety, onions Tk40-45, eggplants Tk50-70, beans Tk150-160, carrots Tk140, tomatoes Tk120 and radishes Tk60.
A wax gourd costs Tk40 each, bananas Tk30 per four, while cauliflower and cabbage are selling for Tk150 and Tk60 respectively.
Vendors at Bahadur Bazar said early vegetable production had been bumper across the district, increasing wholesale supplies and pushing prices down. They said they were buying at lower prices and selling with small profit margins. They expect prices to fall further as winter sets in.
Consumers said the lower prices had reduced their household spending on vegetables. The fall in potato prices has also brought relief to consumers, although importers and traders are facing losses. Farmers, however, are concerned about the price decline.
Several growers in Ghughudanga of Sadar upazila and different areas of Phulbari upazila said favourable weather had resulted in good yields, but current market prices were making it difficult to recover production costs. They fear prices could fall further during the peak season, causing substantial losses.
According to the Department of Agricultural Extension in Dinajpur, the district set a target of cultivating early winter vegetables on more than 7,150 hectares across 13 upazilas this season.
Favourable weather has led to cultivation on more land than targeted, while overall production has also exceeded expectations.

item.title: Murder accused flees court again, cop suspended
item.description:
A murder accused escaped from a Dhaka court for the second time on Tuesday, prompting authorities to suspend the police constable responsible for guarding him and form a three-member committee to investigate the incident.
Shariful fled from the court of Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Md Jamshed Alam on Tuesday. He had also escaped from court custody in 2025, making this his second escape from a Dhaka court.
A case has since been filed against him with Kotwali Police Station over the escape.
Mohiuddin Mahmud Sohel, deputy commissioner of the DMP Prosecution Division, confirmed the matter.
“Shariful, a remanded accused in a case filed with Kotwali Police Station, cleverly slipped out of his handcuffs and escaped from the court. He had been brought from jail as the case was scheduled for a hearing,” he said.
According to Sohel, Shariful took advantage of a moment when the police officer guarding him was distracted and escaped through another door. Police are working to arrest him, he added.
SI Md Morshed Alam, in-charge of the CMM court lock-up, filed the case against Shariful, while Constable Abdul Alim, who was responsible for guarding him, was temporarily suspended.
A three-member committee has also been formed to investigate the incident.
According to the DMP Prosecution Division, Shariful was brought to court on Tuesday for the scheduled hearing, but the proceedings could not take place as the witness failed to appear.
Later, Constable Abdul Alim was taking Shariful to the lock-up when the accused allegedly slipped out of his handcuffs and escaped through another door.
Shariful had previously escaped from court custody on June 19, 2025, while being produced before the Dhaka Third Additional Metropolitan Sessions Judge’s Court in a case over the murder of teenager Jisan Hossain filed with Khilgaon Police Station.
After the hearing, Shariful allegedly assaulted a police officer while being taken from the courtroom to the lock-up, slipped out of his handcuffs and fled.
On the same day, Md Ripon Molla, then in charge of the court lock-up, filed a case against Shariful with Kotwali Police Station over the incident.
Shariful was brought from jail to court on Tuesday in connection with that case.
Shariful is the son of late Shafik Ahmed of Haripur village in Nawabganj upazila of Dinajpur.

item.title: Minister: Fisheries budget must rise while curbing waste
item.description:
Fisheries, Livestock and Agriculture Minister Mohammed Amin Ur Rashid has called for increased budget allocations for the fisheries sector alongside greater transparency, accountability and stronger measures to prevent financial waste.
He made the remarks on Tuesday while speaking as the chief guest at a workshop titled “Budget and Government Development Vision in the Fisheries Sector”, organised by the Department of Fisheries at Matsya Bhaban in Dhaka.
The minister said the country’s identity as “Mache-Bhate Bangali” is deeply connected with the fisheries sector, but the availability of native fish species has declined due to the shrinking of natural water bodies and environmental changes.
He said: “Therefore, alongside boosting production, priority must be given to preserving the natural habitats of fish.”
Emphasising the importance of fish sanctuaries, Amin Ur Rashid said launching projects and spending funds alone would not ensure their effectiveness. He called for regular field-level verification to assess whether sanctuaries are achieving their intended objectives.
“The primary purpose of sanctuaries is to create opportunities for fish breeding and reproduction,” he said, adding that regular reviews were needed to determine how funds were spent, what was achieved and how the initiatives affected overall fish production.
The minister also urged officials to ensure accuracy in the lists of fishermen eligible for government support.
He warned that the inclusion of fake or ineligible beneficiaries could deprive genuine fishermen of government assistance and called on local officials to take greater responsibility during the verification process.
On deep-sea fishing, the minister said Bangladesh has significant potential to commercially harvest tuna and other marine resources in international waters, as several countries are already doing so.
“Instead of merely conducting surveys and spending money, a clear plan is required to translate survey findings into actual marine harvesting,” he said.
He stressed the need to develop skilled manpower, suitable vessels and technological capacity to utilise the country’s deep-sea fishing potential.
State Minister for Fisheries and Livestock Sultan Salauddin Tuku, speaking as the special guest, stressed the need to encourage young entrepreneurs and provide fish farmers with necessary advice and technical support.
He also instructed field-level officials to conduct regular farm inspections and monitor activities.
The state minister said the government is working to increase freshwater fish production, expand exports and bring canals, rivers and other water bodies under fish cultivation.
He identified pollution-free water bodies, maintaining river navigability, improving fish processing facilities and promoting exports as important factors for the sustainable development of the fisheries sector.
Department of Fisheries Director General Dr Md Khaled Kanak chaired the workshop.
Ministry Secretary Md Delwar Hossain attended the event as the honoured guest, while Public Service Commission Member Prof A S M Golam Hafiz participated as the discussant.
Senior officials from the Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock and the Department of Fisheries were also present.

item.title: Editors’ Council calls for end to attacks on journalists
item.description:
The Editors’ Council has expressed deep concern and strongly condemned recent attacks, threats, harassment and obstruction of journalists in different parts of Bangladesh.
The council said the latest attack on journalists at Rajshahi University, while they were performing their professional duties, is particularly concerning. The journalists were collecting information and reporting in the public interest, not on behalf of any particular side.
There is no justification for attacking, threatening, or obstructing journalists, even when there are disagreements over a report, opinion, or a journalist’s professional activities, it added.
“An attack on a journalist is not only an attack on a professional; it is an attack on independent journalism, freedom of expression and the public’s right to know,” it said.
The Editors’ Council welcomed the filing of a case and the initiative to investigate the Rajshahi University incident.
However, it said the investigation must be impartial, credible and evidence-based, and those involved in the attack must be brought to justice regardless of their political or organisational affiliations.
The Editors’ Council made the following demands:
The Editors’ Council said journalists’ safety is not a special privilege but an essential condition for a free, democratic and accountable society.
“Independent journalism is not possible in an environment of fear, threats and violence,” it said, calling on the government, law enforcement agencies, political parties, educational institutions and all relevant stakeholders to take prompt, visible and lawful action in every incident of attack on journalists and adopt effective measures to prevent such incidents in the future.

item.title: PM: Strong children mean a stronger Bangladesh
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Tuesday likened children to the strong pillars of a house, saying Bangladesh’s foundation would become stronger in the competitive world if every child is given the opportunity to develop their abilities properly.
“Children are the pillars of their families. When children are given the right environment and opportunities to grow and flourish, families become stronger,” he while addressing a program marking Children’s Rights Day, 2026 and the 50th anniversary of Bangladesh Shishu Academy on the academy premises in the capital.
In the same way, Tarique said: “If we can ensure opportunities for every child across Bangladesh to develop their full potential, the foundation of our country will become much stronger, enabling Bangladesh to emerge as a strong country in the competitive world.”
He said the government wants to develop children in a way that strengthens their future, as the strength of today’s children will determine the strength of the nation’s future.
“We want to develop our children in a way that makes their future strong. A strong future for today’s children means a strong future for the nation. And a strong future for the nation means we will be able to build a strong and powerful Bangladesh,” the Prime Minister said.
Tarique urged children to develop themselves not only through education but also through sports, Quran recitation, music and other cultural activities.
“You have to become good human beings,” he said, urging children to properly develop the qualities and talents within them.
The prime minister also called on children to be kind to all living beings and caring towards nature and the environment. “People should show kindness not only to other people but also to nature and all of its creations.”
He urged children to care for trees around their homes and schools and to be kind to birds and animals, describing them as national assets.
Tarique also called on guardians to help children develop a sense of responsibility towards nature from an early age.
“If we are kind to nature, nature will also be kind to us,” he said, urging children and guardians to work together to protect the environment.
The prime minister also asked children to play a role in keeping their surroundings clean. He urged them to politely remind adults not to throw waste indiscriminately and to use designated places for disposing of rubbish.
“If we can build a clean and beautiful environment today, your children will grow up in a healthy environment, both physically and mentally,” he said.
The prime minister said the government is working to provide children across the country with opportunities to develop their talents in sports, arts, culture and music, particularly because many families cannot afford such facilities.
He said the government has recently organised a football competition at the primary-school level in which around 2.2 million children — 1.1 million boys and 1.1 million girls — participated.
“If we can continue this, I firmly believe that one day a Pele or internationally recognised players will emerge from among our children,” he said.
The prime minister also recalled the “Notun Kuri” program introduced by Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman to nurture children’s cultural talents, saying the government has revived it while also launching similar initiatives in sports.
He said sports activities have also been initiated alongside cultural programs, with events being organised at the national level.
“We want our children to have good exposure to art, culture and music, while also becoming capable in sports,” Tarique said, adding that every child has some quality or talent that needs to be given an opportunity to flourish.
The prime minister said the government is working to introduce facilities at schools so that children, including those in remote and rural areas, can choose activities according to their interests.
He said the government plans to provide opportunities from the primary and secondary levels for children to learn music, play musical instruments and participate in different sports.
“We want to develop children in this way to make their future stronger,” the Prime Minister said.
Tarique also announced plans to introduce opportunities for children to learn a third foreign language alongside Bangla and English.
He said students would be able to choose from several languages, potentially including Arabic, Mandarin and German, to help them in higher education and employment abroad.
“Learning a third foreign language will help them stand firmly in life and compete with people from other countries,” Tarique said.
The prime minister, however, stressed that academic achievement, sports, cultural activities or learning several languages alone would not be enough.“Dear little friends, you have many responsibilities. You have to be humane,” he said.
Earlier, around 150 children welcomed the prime minister when he arrived at Bangladesh Shishu Academy. The program began with the national anthem.
Prime minister’s wife and Ziaur Rahman Foundation Vice-Chairman Dr Zubaida Rahman attended the program, chaired by Women and Children Affairs Minister Prof Dr AZM Zahid Hossain.
The prime minister enjoyed cultural performances by children and later interacted with the performers and took part in a photo session. He also answered questions from children.
Children from different parts of the country also interacted with the prime minister through videoconference.
Tarique later visited an exhibition of paintings by children and a photo gallery at the Children’s Museum building and inaugurated a solar panel system and a substation on its ground floor.
Earlier, children presented him with a commemorative gift, while he unveiled the special souvenir Shaishab.
This year’s program is being held under the theme “Let every child have a secure future.”

item.title: Dhanmondi Lake restoration begins, 'Nazrul Sarobar' in plan
item.description:
Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC) has begun dredging Dhanmondi Lake as part of an extensive development program aimed at restoring its navigability, environmental quality and recreational facilities.
The dredging work was inaugurated on Tuesday morning by DSCC Administrator Md Abdus Salam and Road Transport and Bridges Minister and local lawmaker Sheikh Rabiul Alam.
The 3.10-km-long lake has an average width of 56 metres and an estimated 162,534 cubic metres of accumulated sludge, including mud and waste.
Two floating excavators and four barges will be used to remove around 700 cubic metres of sludge daily. The dredging is expected to take about a year and initially cost Tk26 crore.
The site covers around 86 acres, including about 55 acres of water body. The lake was developed in the 1960s from the remnants of the old Pandu River.
Speaking at the inauguration, Sheikh Rabiul Alam said the development and management of Dhanmondi Lake had been one of his election pledges.
“The prime minister has approved two projects in this regard. As the first phase, sludge removal from the lake began today (Tuesday). The entire lake will be renovated according to the detailed design,” he said.
He also urged visitors and local residents to remain conscious of their responsibility to protect the lake’s environment.
DSCC Administrator Md Abdus Salam said several development works would begin after the lakebed is cleaned.
“Immediately after cleaning the lakebed, water treatment, sidewall renovation, modernisation and expansion of the walkway, beautification and lighting works will begin,” he said.
He said facilities including speedboat rides for children would also be introduced, while roads, footpaths and other infrastructure in the Dhanmondi area would be improved.
An open cultural and recreational centre named “Nazrul Sarobar”, modelled on Rabindra Sarobar, will also be developed as part of the initiative.
The DSCC has prepared a Tk75 crore master plan to restore Dhanmondi Lake and develop it as a recreational destination while addressing long-standing waterlogging, infrastructure and environmental problems.
Of the total allocation, Tk50 crore has been earmarked for renovating the lake and related infrastructure, while Tk25 crore will be spent on the proposed “Nazrul Sarobar” or “Bidrohi Chattar”.
The wider plan includes strengthening the lake’s banks and stabilising its slopes, improving drainage, renovating walkways and repairing boundary fencing and safety railings.
It also includes improved lighting, CCTV cameras, a public announcement system and directional signboards.
The master plan proposes three floating decks, kiosks, a modern gym, cafeteria, badminton court, open-air gymnasium and parking facilities.
It also includes a specialised “tree hospital” for plant maintenance, safe drinking water facilities and public toilets.
The proposed Nazrul Sarobar will be developed on 50.967 kathas of land beside Road 13/A and Road 8/A in Dhanmondi, opposite the Kazi Nazrul Islam Institute.
The Tk25 crore cultural space will feature an open-air amphitheatre and green room for Nazrul songs, cultural programs and discussions.
It will also include a book corner, library, information panels, urban forest, plaza and a lake ghat highlighting the life, literary works and rebellious spirit of National Poet Kazi Nazrul Islam.
A restaurant and café serving some of Nazrul’s favourite foods are also planned.
According to the development plan, the main lake renovation and construction of Nazrul Sarobar will be carried out simultaneously after sludge removal is completed.
The authorities expect the project to address the lake’s long-standing environmental and infrastructure problems while creating a safer and more accessible recreational and cultural space in one of Dhaka’s major urban areas.

item.title: Measles outbreak: Death toll rises to 1,134 as 6 children die 24hrs
item.description:
Six more children died with measles-like symptoms in 24 hours until 8am on Tuesday, bringing the country’s combined tally of confirmed and suspected measles-related deaths to 1,134 this year.
The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) has classified all six latest fatalities as suspected measles deaths.
With these, the total number of suspected measles deaths has reached 1,032, while confirmed deaths from measles have remained the same at 102, it said.
A total of 1,291 new suspected measles cases were reported during the 24 hours, bringing the cumulative number of suspected cases nationwide to 199,013
Meanwhile, 102 new confirmed measles cases were recorded, bringing the total number of laboratory-confirmed infections to 21,910.
Since March 15 this year, a total of 176,516 patients with suspected measles have been hospitalised across the country, of whom 169,290 have recovered, according to DGHS data.

item.title: DCs ordered to ensure LPG, autogas sales at BERC-set prices
item.description:
All deputy commissioners (DCs) have been instructed to take necessary measures to keep LPG supplies normal in the open market and ensure that LPG and autogas are sold at the prices set by the Bangladesh Energy Regulatory Commission (BERC), said Information and Broadcasting Adviser Dr Zahed Ur Rahman on Tuesday.
The government has intensified monitoring across the country to ensure the sale of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) and autogas at prices fixed by the commission amid volatility in international fuel prices, he said at a press briefing held at the Secretariat on the progress of various government activities.
Fuel prices in the international market remain highly volatile, while the government is trying to adjust LPG prices accordingly, he said adding “However, there have been complaints that LPG is not available at the adjusted prices in some places,” he said.
The energy and mineral resources minister held an online meeting with the DCs and issued necessary directives in this regard, he added.
Monitoring is also being conducted in different districts through mobile courts operated by the Directorate of National Consumer Rights Protection and local administrations, he said.
“Earlier, many were fined. Now, these monitoring activities have been intensified further,” the adviser said.
The government is also holding discussions with LPG traders to improve the market situation, he said.
The energy minister has held several meetings with leaders of LPG-related businesses to review the situation, Zahed said, adding that the traders assured the minister of their cooperation in keeping the market stable.
The government hopes the current crisis in the LPG market will ease through these efforts, he said.
Zahed urged the media to highlight any complaints about LPG not being available at the government-fixed prices.
“If LPG is still unavailable at the fixed price anywhere, the media will highlight the issue in the public interest, and the government will take necessary action. LPG is an extremely essential product. In fact, it is not possible to manage without it,” the adviser said.

item.title: Son: Wife of jailed ex-Venezuelan leader Maduro has ‘very delicate’ heart issue
item.description:
Venezuelan former first lady Cilia Flores has a “very delicate” heart condition, her son-in-law told AFP on Monday, calling for her release from the US prison where she was jailed alongside Nicolas Maduro.
Flores, 69, was arrested alongside Maduro by US forces during a raid on Caracas on January 3 and taken to the United States to face trial on drug trafficking charges.
She is being held in the same federal prison in Brooklyn, New York, as ousted socialist president Maduro, 63.
Last month, her lawyer requested she be placed under house arrest, saying that she suffers from heart problems for which her prison conditions do not provide adequate care.
The US government opposed the request, arguing she posed “an extreme risk of flight and danger to the public.”
Maduro’s son, Nicolas Maduro Guerra, told AFP that Flores is suffering from a “prolapsed” heart, a condition that, in rare, severe cases, can cause heart failure.
He said that she required surgery and needed to be released from jail in order to properly recuperate afterwards.
Flores’ lawyer Mark Donnelly suggested she be placed under house arrest with 24-hour armed surveillance, an electronic monitoring bracelet and that her passport be confiscated.
Flores, a former president of the National Assembly and attorney general, was seen as a key figure with the repressive Maduro regime.
Both she and Maduro are accused of helping traffic cocaine into the United States, which they deny.
The pair are scheduled to go on trial on June 1, 2027.
Maduro has asked for the charges against him to be dismissed, invoking his immunity as head of state.
In 2015, two of Flores’ nephews were arrested by US officials in Haiti on charges of attempting to traffic cocaine to the United States.
Franqui Francisco Flores de Freitas and Efrain Antonio Campos Flores were each sentenced to 18 years in prison in 2017 but were released in 2022 as part of a prisoner swap deal with the administration of former president Joe Biden.
After Maduro’s ouster, his former deputy Delcy Rodriguez took over as interim president, with the backing of US President Donald Trump.
Rodriguez has appeared ready to comply with Trump’s agenda in Venezuela, including his bid to control vast chunks of the country’s huge oil reserves.

India opposition leaders briefly detained in election protest
item.description:
India’s opposition leader Rahul Gandhi was briefly detained by police on Tuesday during a march protesting against the Election Commission, demanding its chief resign and alleging wrongdoing during a revision of voter rolls.
An AFP reporter saw Gandhi, a leader of the Congress Party, standing on a police barricade and waving an Indian flag. Officers detained him briefly, along with other lawmakers, and then released them soon after.
Opposition parties began their march from parliament towards to the Election Commission of India (ECI), but were stopped by heavy police deployments. Some politicians sat down on the street to wait.
Protests began on Friday, demanding that commission chief Gyanesh Kumar step down.
Opposition politicians have accused the commission of acting at the behest of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party.
The ECI has rejected allegations of wrongdoing, saying the revision process is aimed at ensuring the accuracy and integrity of electoral rolls.
Kumar has not commented publicly.
“Gyanesh, it’s done, bro,” placards read, as well as signs alleging electoral manipulation.
Opposition leaders pressed their demands for greater transparency in the revision of voter lists, alleging that changes to the rolls could disenfranchise eligible voters.
The protest was part of a wider campaign against the Election Commission’s Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.
The issue of voter deletion was reignited by a report in September by The Indian Express newspaper, which said two of the ECI’s three members had formally objected at least 14 times to key decisions linked to the voter roll revision.
The news report claimed the names of 130 million citizens had been deleted since the exercise began in 2025.

item.title: Dengue cases surge in Chittagong, 21 deaths recorded this year
item.description:
The dengue outbreak in Chittagong is intensifying, with 4,914 infections and 21 deaths recorded in the district between January 1 and October 5.
The situation worsened sharply in September, when 2,430 cases and 16 deaths were reported.
According to the District Civil Surgeon’s Office, 107 new dengue cases were detected in the 24 hours until 8am on Sunday. Of the 4,914 patients recorded this year, 260 are currently undergoing treatment at different hospitals, while 4,654 have recovered and been discharged.
The dengue situation remained relatively mild at the beginning of the year, with 68 cases in January, 22 in February, 20 in March, 29 in April and 37 in May.
Cases began rising in June, reaching 122 that month, followed by 536 in July and 1,202 in August. The number surged to 2,430 in September.
Another 448 cases were reported in the first five days of October.
September was also the deadliest month, accounting for 16 of the 21 deaths recorded this year. Two deaths each were reported in July and August, while one was recorded in February.
No new dengue deaths were reported in the 24 hours preceding the latest update.
According to data from the District Civil Surgeon’s Office, 2,285 of the 4,914 cases were reported in Chittagong city, 2,098 in different upazilas and 531 among patients who came from other districts.
Among the upazilas, Sitakunda recorded the highest number of cases at 620, followed by Karnaphuli with 285, Banshkhali 154, Rangunia 152, Satkania 121, Anwara 112, Raozan 103 and Patiya 100.
Other cases were reported in Hathazari (84), Chandanaish (77), Boalkhali (76), Mirsharai (79), Lohagara (66), Fatikchhari (44) and Sandwip (25).
Of the total dengue patients recorded this year, 2,402 are men, 1,403 are women and 1,109 are children.
Among the 107 patients admitted in the 24-hour period, 56 were men, 23 were women and 28 were children.
However, women accounted for the highest number of deaths. Of the 21 people who died, 11 were women, six were children and four were men.
The number of dengue cases recorded in Chittagong this year has already surpassed the totals for the previous two years.
The district recorded 4,323 cases and 45 deaths in 2024, while 4,864 cases and 27 deaths were reported in 2025.
As of October 5 this year, the number of cases stood at 4,914, with 21 deaths.
Residents have complained that mosquito-control activities in Chittagong have not kept pace with the rising number of dengue cases.
Muntasir Uddin, a resident of Sangeet Residential Area in Hamzarbag, said mosquito infestations in the area had become severe, while City Corporation workers assigned to mosquito control were rarely seen.
He also alleged a lack of supervision over the effectiveness of insecticide spraying.
Jamal Uddin, a resident of Chandanpura, said the number of dengue patients in the city had increased significantly, but City Corporation monitoring had not increased proportionately.
District Civil Surgeon Mohammad Sajedur Rahman told Bangla Tribune that dengue is a mosquito-borne disease and urged residents to keep their surroundings clean.
He said dengue could be controlled by destroying mosquito breeding grounds and advised people to undergo dengue tests and seek medical advice promptly if they develop a fever.
Sheikh Fazle Rabbi, divisional director of health in Chittagong, also advised people to consult a doctor immediately if they develop fever or symptoms of dengue.
He said the most important measure to prevent dengue was to destroy Aedes mosquito breeding grounds, while efforts should also be made to eliminate adult mosquitoes.
He said the City Corporation had been sent several letters urging it to intensify mosquito-control activities.
Ashraful Amin, chief executive officer and secretary of Chittagong City Corporation, told Bangla Tribune that the corporation was conducting regular mosquito-control activities to combat dengue and other mosquito-borne diseases.
He said special “crash programmes” were also being conducted in different areas when necessary.
Amin said dengue could not be controlled through insecticide spraying alone and stressed the need to destroy mosquito breeding grounds.
He also urged residents to prevent water from stagnating in and around their homes, rooftops, construction sites and other areas.

Dhaka ranks first globally in air pollution
item.description:
Dhaka ranked first among the world's most polluted cities on Tuesday morning, recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 213 at 11:10am.
The air quality was classified as "very unhealthy", signalling a serious health alert where everyone may experience health effects, according to the AQI scale.
Kuala Lumpur in Malaysia ranked second with an AQI score of 208, while Singapore in Singapore ranked third with a score of 179 and Kolkata in India ranked fourth with an AQI score of 177.
According to AQI standards, a reading between 101 and 150 is considered "unhealthy for sensitive groups", while 151 to 200 is classified as "unhealthy". A reading between 201 and 300 is considered "very unhealthy", while levels above 301 are deemed "hazardous", posing serious health risks.
The AQI provides daily updates on air quality, indicating how clean or polluted the air is and highlighting potential health impacts.
In Bangladesh, the AQI is calculated based on five major pollutants: particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO2) and ozone.
Dhaka has long struggled with air pollution, with air quality typically deteriorating during winter and improving during the monsoon season.
The World Health Organization estimates that air pollution causes around seven million deaths globally each year, mainly from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer and acute respiratory infections.

COP31 eyes modest steps as climate disasters multiply
item.description:
Nations reeling from a year of climate devastation gather for COP31 next month, but negotiations are not expected to deliver major progress in cutting the fossil fuels driving the crisis.
The conference follows deadly heatwaves and fires in Europe, catastrophic floods in Nepal and record temperatures around the world, testing whether the United Nations-backed talks can keep pace with reality.
As leaders meet in Turkey, an exceptionally powerful El Niño pattern will be approaching peak strength, threatening to amplify weather chaos worldwide and drive global heat to unprecedented highs.
Concerns over energy security will also loom large, with no end in sight to the Middle East war that has sent oil and gas prices soaring and hit fossil fuel-importing nations hard.
With a new agreement on fossil fuels unlikely, Turkey is rallying support for a voluntary "electrification" pledge it says could cut heat-trapping emissions and reduce reliance on energy imports.
"In many ways, the defining contexts for this year's climate summit will be heat and Hormuz," said David Waskow from the World Resources Institute, referencing the vital strait that carried one-fifth of the world's hydrocarbons before the Iran war.
Unusually, Turkey must navigate these complexities with Australia, a major fossil fuel exporter, after both countries agreed to share COP31 duties following a bruising hosting battle.
Australia's Climate Minister Chris Bowen, who is leading the negotiations in Antalya starting November 9, said this year's extreme events "show climate change is not a future challenge".
"It is a present reality... and the costs of inaction are rising," he said.
A "pre-COP" meeting began Monday in the climate-vulnerable Pacific with a leaders' retreat in Tuvalu and government meetings in Fiji.
Unlike recent COPs -- where nearly 200 nations forged landmark pacts on phasing down coal or moving away from fossil fuels -- the negotiation agenda at COP31 is light on big-ticket items.
There are more than 100 items on the table but many deal with technical matters, like approving indicators to track progress on climate adaptation.
"Much of the Antalya summit will be a 'roll up the sleeves' effort. Governments need to make concrete headway in negotiations, though there may not be dramatic outcomes this year," Waskow told AFP.
Nations are not expected to adopt new binding commitments to reduce the burning of fossil fuels -- the leading cause of climate change.
Countries agreed in 2023 to move away from coal, oil and gas but since then efforts to negotiate concrete targets or timelines for that transition have gone nowhere.
At last year's summit, fossil fuels were not mentioned by name in the final agreement after oil and gas-producing nations prevented consensus on the issue.
"Everyone agrees there will be no real gain at the multilateral level at the moment," Marta Torres-Gunfaus from the IDDRI think tank told AFP.
Fossil fuel emissions, meanwhile, hit record highs in 2025.
In September, the UN conceded that the milestone 1.5C climate target will be missed in a matter of years.
Nations frustrated at the COP gridlock have sought progress elsewhere.
Nearly 60 countries attended a fossil fuel phaseout conference without UN involvement this year.
France, the Netherlands and Germany have published "roadmaps" with explicit deadlines for quitting coal, oil and gas.
UN Climate chief Simon Stiell has defended the negotiations while acknowledging their limitations: "No single COP can fix this global crisis, but each takes meaningful steps forward," he said.
Turkey says it is not realistic to expect all countries to move at the same pace.
"Any proposal that fails to reconcile our climate objectives with social and economic realities will be doomed to fail," said Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
Turkey is curating an "action agenda" alongside the negotiations that encourages countries to support non-binding pledges on issues from artificial intelligence to waste management.
There is broad support for its centrepiece goal: raising the share of global energy demand met by electricity from around 20% on Tuesday to 35% by 2035.
The electrification target does not state how that extra power should be produced. One-third of electricity is generated by coal, and there are concerns the target could provide cover for expanded fossil fuel use.
The Nepal floods would also put "a huge amount of pressure" on western countries to increase financial support for climate disaster recovery, said Ajay Mathur, a former Indian government negotiator.
"We did not create this crisis, yet we are paying for it," Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah said.

Tangail eyes tourism boom with rich heritage and natural beauty
item.description:
Rich in history, cultural heritage, and natural beauty, Tangail has vast potential to develop as a major tourism destination, with its historic landmarks, forests, traditional handloom industry, and distinctive products offering a diverse experience for visitors.
The district is home to Mughal-era Atia Mosque, Mohera, Hemnagar, Karotia, Delduar, Pakutia, and Dhanbari zamindar mansions, Madhupur National Park, Pirgachha Rubber Garden, and Jamuna Bridge. Its proximity to Dhaka and relatively easy road connectivity further enhance its prospects as a tourism hub.
Tourism could also generate employment for local guides, resort operators, restaurants, and handicraft businesses while creating opportunities for increased local revenue through public-private investment.
Among the district's natural attractions, Madhupur National Park stands out for its extensive forest landscape and wildlife. Spread across more than 20,000 acres, the park offers visitors a break from urban life. It is also home to a deer breeding centre.
Pirgachha Rubber Garden in Madhupur is another popular destination. Visitors can enjoy the changing appearance of its large rubber trees across the seasons and, with permission, observe the process of collecting and processing raw rubber at a nearby factory.
Atia Mosque in Delduar is one of Tangail's notable historical landmarks. Built in a distinctive Mughal-Sultanate architectural style, the single-domed mosque was once featured on the Tk10 banknote. The 201-domed mosque in Gopalpur is another attraction, featuring eight tall minarets, four of which are 101 feet high.
The Jamuna Bridge area in Kalihati draws visitors for its river views, open air, and sunrise and sunset scenes. The nearby Jamuna Railway Bridge has also become an attraction.
Upendra Sarobar in Nagarpur, around 25km from Tangail town, is another scenic destination. The lake, locally known as “Baro Ghatla Dighi,” has 12 ghats and was excavated in 1341 Bengali calendar to address the area's drinking water shortage.
Tangail's cultural identity is further strengthened by Porabari Chamcham, a traditional sweet with a history of around two centuries, and its famous handloom sarees. Visitors can explore the district's historic zamindar mansions, particularly Mohera Zamindar Bari, one of the most popular heritage sites.
Local residents say the tourism sector needs better preservation of historical sites, quality hotels, and resorts, improved security, and stronger digital promotion to reach domestic and international tourists.
Tangail Deputy Commissioner Sharifa Haque said the district's 12 upazilas offered diverse natural and cultural attractions. “Tourism can play an important role in the local economy. We have to present Tangail's history, heritage, culture, and natural beauty to the world, and we are working towards that goal,” she said.
Local lawmaker and State Minister Sultan Salahuddin Tuku said plans were underway to develop Tangail as a modern tourism hub, including a mini tourism centre around the DC Lake and a larger tourism destination in the char areas.
He said improved connectivity, cleanliness, scenic development, and tourist facilities would be essential to unlock the district's tourism potential and create more employment opportunities.

item.title: Case filed over attack on journalists at RU
item.description:
A case was filed against unidentified people on Monday over an attack on journalists on the Rajshahi University (RU) campus allegedly by leaders and activists of Bangladesh Jatiyatabadi Chhatra Dal (JCD).
Md Munir Hossain, deputy registrar of Shaheed Ziaur Rahman Hall, filed the case with Motihar Police Station, said its Officer-in-Charge Golam Kabir.
“We have recorded a case. We have started working on it and will take action after investigation,” he said.
However, journalists covering the university expressed dissatisfaction over the decision to file the case against unidentified suspects.
They demanded that those involved in the attack be identified and arrested quickly and that the university administration take visible and effective action against them.
Ashiqul Islam Dhrubo, president of RU Press Club, said there was no ambiguity about the identities of those involved in the attack.
“We have all the footage of the attack, and people across the country have seen it. It is as clear as daylight who was involved. Their names, posts and identities have already been published in news reports,” he said.
“There is no question of filing a case against unidentified persons. We demand that the names of everyone involved be included in the case and that they be arrested as soon as possible,” Ashiqul added.
Former RU Journalists’ Association President Irfan Tamim also criticised the decision, describing it as extremely disappointing.
Ten people, including four journalists, were injured when JCD leaders and activists allegedly attacked them in front of Shaheed Ziaur Rahman Hall around 8:30pm on Sunday.
Several JCD leaders and activists, including university unit Vice-President Ahsan Habib, were alleged to have been involved in the attack.
The attack reportedly took place after journalists took photographs of locally made weapons allegedly displayed for an attack on a rival group.
The injured journalists include Arifuzzaman Qurban, RU correspondent of bdnews24.com; Zahidul Islam, correspondent of Agamir Somoy; Noor Ahsan Mridul, correspondent of The Daily Star; and Mainul Islam Raju, correspondent of Samakal.
Meanwhile, a five-member committee was formed to investigate the incident.

item.title: Remittance inflows up over 15% in current FY27
item.description:
Bangladesh has received $8.798 billion in remittances so far in FY27, sent to the country between July 1 and October 3.
This represents a 15.1% increase compared to the $7.643 billion received during the same period of the previous fiscal year.
Executive spokesperson of Bangladesh Bank Arief Hossain Khan confirmed the data on Sunday (October 4).
He noted that the significant growth in remittances was driven by an increase in funds sent home by Bangladeshi expatriate workers during the first few months of the current fiscal year.
According to Bangladesh Bank data, the country’s gross foreign exchange reserves stood at approximately $36.14 billion as of September 29.
Earlier on September 20, total foreign exchange reserves were at $36.30 billion.
According to the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) BPM6 calculation method at that time, the reserve amount was $31.45 billion.
According to the central bank's updated report, remittances worth $1.877 billion arrived in the country during the first 20 days of September.
Of this, expatriates sent $130 million in just three days—from September 17 to 19—compared to $1.869 billion received in the first 19 days of September last year.

item.title: Experts: Bangladesh poultry must shift from volume to value
item.description:
Speakers at the International Technical Seminar 2026 organized by the World's Poultry Science Association – Bangladesh Branch (WPSA-BB) emphasized that Bangladesh's poultry sector must move beyond a volume-centric mindset and focus on farm profitability, food safety, climate resilience, and internationally credible standards.
Held under the theme "Resilient Poultry Production for Global Competitiveness", the seminar featured eight speakers representing the government, industry, and academia.
Md Shahzaman Khan, director general, Department of Livestock Services (DLS), attended the inaugural session as chief guest.
Special guests included Moshiur Rahman, convener, Bangladesh Poultry Industries Central Council (BPICC), and Shakila Faruque, director general, Bangladesh Livestock Research Institute (BLRI).
The session was chaired by WPSA-BB president Shamsul Arefin Khaled.
WPSA-BB president Shamsul Arefin Khaled stated that while the sector has addressed volume growth, it has yet to secure value realization.
Despite rising output, many producers are incurring losses; according to his estimates, breeder farms lost approximately Tk1,706 crore over the past 20 months.
He highlighted that profit margins have shifted from farms and hatcheries to intermediaries along the supply chain.
He urged aligning chick supply with market demand, according legal status to the national poultry policy, and expanding investments in insurance, processing, and cold chains.
Ensuring farmer protection and building a sustainable industry: WPSA-BB general secretary Fayzur Rahman outlined the strategic direction for the industry.
Md Zahidul Islam, director & CEO of Bangla-UK Agro Products Ltd, noted that the lowest FCR does not always yield the highest profitability. Adhering strictly to drug withdrawal periods and marketing heavier birds can improve farm income as well as food safety.
Khitima Jindamongkon, regional manager at dsm-firmenich APAC, shared insights from Asian poultry industries, noting that future success depends on integration, processing, traceability, and leveraging local breeds like the 'Sonali' chicken.
Prof Emdadul Haque Chowdhury, Department of Pathology at Bangladesh Agricultural University (BAU), presented a research study combining consumer/stakeholder surveys with laboratory testing. Contrary to public misconceptions, no growth hormones were detected in the tested samples.
Moshiur Rahman, managing director of Paragon Group and convener of BPICC, stated that optimizing feed conversion, efficient energy management, and reducing mortality can lower both operational costs and carbon emissions.
Baby Rani Karmakar, joint secretary at the Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock, noted that while Bangladesh can compete in international halal markets, success requires internationally recognized certification, accredited laboratories, and market-specific compliance frameworks.
The seminar concluded with an open discussion titled "Towards a Globally Competitive, Safe, and Sustainable Poultry Sector in Bangladesh", moderated by Prof Md Mahmudul Hasan Sikder, member-secretary of the WPSA-BB technical sub-committee.
Discussions also focused on developing affordable, smart, resource-efficient farming models across scales and charting the strategic roadmap for the sector.
